newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya defends closure of supermarket chain.
newsitem.headline: Kenya defends closure of supermarket chain.

text.p: One of Kenya's biggest supermarket chains will remain closed on evidence that it imported possibly contaminated beef from Britain, Commerce and Industry Minister Kirugi M'Mukindia said on Wednesday.

"This beef is banned from importation to this country. If there is any indication of the worst form of capitalism, it is where a knowledgeable person, knowing the effects of the 'mad cow' disease, imports the same to be sold to people," M'Mukindia told a news conference in Nairobi.

Nakumatt Holdings' eight stores in Kenya were closed on September 19 when its trading licences were revoked on grounds it imported without proper approval 3.2 tonnes of corned beef from Britain, which has had outbreaks of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or "mad cow" disease.
Nakumatt Holdings Ltd took full-page advertisements in Kenyan newspapers on Tuesday to publish a statement saying a mad cow disease scare was a pretext.
It said just before the closures it refused to pay a bribe of 50 million shillings ($893,000), demanded by an anonymous telephone caller, and linked its problems with anti-Asian sentiment.
It said the corned beef was from Brazil and packed there by British company John West and then exported to Kenya. John West confirmed this in a statement issued in London on Tuesday.

"Locally reared beef is used by our Brazilian supplier and this is not in any way associated with BSE," said the statement by John West, a subsidiary of the Unilever Group. "There is no reason why this consignment should be held."
The company declined further comment on Wednesday.
A senior Nakumatt source told Reuters the company had no immediate comment on M'Mukindia's statements on Wednesday.

M'Mukindia rejected as "traders' talk" the Nakumatt and John West statements: "On the basis of the evidence I have, this beef certainly comes from Britain. John West has made a statement, so has Nakumatt, they are all traders: traders talk. Kenya is not a dumping ground for poisons and this must be very clear."
He also rejected Nakumatt claims that it was targetted because it was owned by Kenyan Asians, and said Nakumatt should have reported to the police any blackmail attempts.
